Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Liam Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Liam from Redwood, AE.
[00:00:06] Liam Patel: With me is Avery Chen, our solutions engineer, we'll run through performance constraints and then map out a benchmark plan.
[00:00:14] Dr. Mira Sol: Hey! thanks. Mira here. High level we run NovaQuant's interactive analytics chat, and then heavier researcher jobs. Latency is, like, super important for the chat product. We're targeting p95 under 300 milliseconds for short replies — that includes network hop, so we need to understand hosted latencies.
[00:00:32] Avery Chen: Got it. 300ms p95 is tight but we can scope it. Are your short replies ~8–20 tokens on average, or longer?
[00:00:39] Dr. Mira Sol: Usually 10 tokens, like short clarification responses. Tom can add details on concurrency.
[00:00:44] Tom Becker: Yes. During business hours we see steady-state ~1k concurrent short sessions, each making a request every 6–8 seconds. Then we have scheduled research runs where we hit bursts up to 5k concurrent short requests for about 10–15 minutes.
[00:01:00] Liam Patel: Helpful. So steady-state 1k conc, bursts to 5k — and p95 300ms for short responses.
[00:01:07] Diego Ramos: One constraint: our data must not leave the EU and keys are managed in our HSM. We're evaluating private deployment but want to understand Dedicated first for cost predictability.
[00:01:20] Priya Nair: Also SOC 2 is required, and our SSO is S A M L with SCIM provisioning. We need audit logs and token-level cost breakdowns for chargeback.
[00:01:32] Avery Chen: Understood — we support SAML/SCIM, KMS integrations, and provide audit logs in the Console. For Dedicated we can provide regional isolation; Private is the fully customer-managed plane with KMS/HSM local.
[00:01:46] Dr. Mira Sol: Great. On latency: how much of the p95 is typically serving runtime vs network? We're trying to budget 150–200ms for backend, 100–150ms for network and app.
[00:01:58] Avery Chen: It's model-dependent. For a 13B OPT-family style model, with optimized kernels and warmed KV cache, per-token generation is small — but streaming adds overhead. For 10-token short responses, the dominant cost is p99-ish attention/memory overhead for first token. We usually look at p95 per-request end-to-end. For Hosted we publish benchmarks but network variability can swing. Dedicated in-region reduces that variability.
[00:02:20] Liam Patel: To be concrete, our playbook: run a token/sec microbenchmark with both streaming and non-streaming, measure cold vs warm KV cache, and then map to request shapes you provide. We'll include p50/p95/p99 and token/sec.
[00:02:34] Tom Becker: What's the recommended model family? We plan to start with an open 13B and possibly 70B for certain research flows. Costwise 70B is heavy.
[00:02:43] Avery Chen: For your latency targets, 13B optimized and quantized (4-bit QAT or Q4/8 depending) is likely the sweet spot. 70B can handle longer context but the tail latency jumps. We can provide quantization profiles.
[00:02:57] Dr. Mira Sol: Okay. For KV cache warming: our traffic is fairly bursty — it may be cold at burst start. How does Redwood handle prefix caching and multi-tenant cache warming?
[00:03:09] Avery Chen: We do prefix/KV caching per-customer; Dedicated gives more control over cache warming policies. For Hosted we can pre-warm shared caches by priming routines but it's less deterministic. We'll run experiments: measure cold start p95 at t0 and after warm-up while simulating your traffic.
[00:03:25] [00:03:26] Diego Ramos: Quick question, are you able to do continuous batching while streaming? We need near-real-time so long batching is not acceptable but micro-batching helps throughput.
[00:03:36] Avery Chen: We support continuous batching with latency SLO knobs — small batches, prioritized low-latency queues for chat. We can show a sample config: target batch size 1–8 for low latency, with opportunistic batching for the rest. We'll include those numbers in the benchmark sheet.
[00:03:49] [00:03:50] Priya Nair: On security, can you describe key rotation cadence and whether logs include per-request key-id?
[00:03:58] Liam Patel: We integrate with customer KMS; key rotation cadence is up to you when using Private. For Dedicated we can bring KMS in-region and rotate per your policy; we capture audit trails with key IDs but we'll confirm the exact granularity in the security pack.
[00:04:12] Tom Becker: For burst scenarios, what's the approach for graceful degradation? We can't drop to 3s latencies.
[00:04:20] Avery Chen: We offer routing policies — during capacity constraints you can failover to a smaller model variant or to a lower-cost Dedicated pool. Also automatic rate-limiting and queue-based prioritization. For critical short-chat traffic you can reserve a percent of capacity.
[00:04:33] Dr. Mira Sol: Can you do canary deploys across Dedicated and Hosted? We want to roll a model gradually.
[00:04:39] Avery Chen: Yes, rollouts and canaries are first-class in the Console; you can split traffic, measure latency regressions on your probes, and automatic fallback if p95 exceeds threshold.
[00:04:48] [00:04:50] Diego Ramos: I want to talk numbers — token/sec and p95 mapping.
[00:04:53] Liam Patel: Sure. For 13B on a single A100-ish GPU with optimizations, warm token throughput might be ~600–1200 tokens/sec depending on quant and kernel, streaming reduces effective throughput per user. So for 1k concurrent short requests (10 tokens each every ~6s) that maps to: 1k users * (10 tokens / 6s) = ~1.67k tokens/sec sustained. That suggests we'd need multiple gpus / nodes.
[00:05:18] Avery Chen: Right. With continuous batching and KV cache we can improve amortized cost. We'll run a spreadsheet scenario: map tokens/sec target to nodes with your prompt distribution. We'll include p95 latency projections per node count.
[00:05:30] Tom Becker: How does streaming add latency per token? For small messages if we flush per token, do we see big overhead?
[00:05:36] Avery Chen: There's some per-chunk overhead and network flushes; often we stream in small chunks (2–4 tokens) to balance interactivity and overhead. We'll include streaming chunk size experiments.
[00:05:47] Dr. Mira Sol: Are the benchmarks you share reproducible on-prem? We may need to run them in our air-gapped environment.
[00:05:54] Avery Chen: Yes — we provide a benchmark harness and config scripts. For Private deployments we can hand over the harness and help run it with your ops team.
[00:06:01] [00:06:05] Priya Nair: One more: do you have SOC 2 Type II and penetration test reports?
[00:06:09] Liam Patel: Yes, we have SOC 2 and pen tests; I'll share the security pack. For Private we can align to your internal audit process.
[00:06:18] Diego Ramos: Pricing question: Dedicated reserved vs burstable — how do we think about the economics for 1k steady conc + bursts to 5k?
[00:06:25] Liam Patel: We'll provide a cost model in the spreadsheet: reserved nodes for steady load and burst capacity for ephemeral on-demand. Dedicated reserved is cheaper per-token but you pay commit. We'll layout scenarios: reserved for baseline, on-demand for peaks, and fallbacks to smaller model variants.
[00:06:39] Tom Becker: Can you also include tracing hooks so we can tie p95 regressions to specific prompts?
[00:06:44] Avery Chen: Yes, Console supports tracing, and you can attach prompt identifiers and tags — we can surface prompt-level SLO breakdowns.
[00:06:52] Dr. Mira Sol: Awesome. I also want to ensure data never leaves region and logs are encrypted with our key.
[00:06:58] Liam Patel: For Private it's straightforward; for Dedicated we can do in-region and integrate with your KMS. We'll put the exact architecture in the deep-dive.
[00:07:06] [00:07:07] Diego Ramos: For the benchmark sheet, include columns: model, gpu type, quantization, warm/cold, stream chunk size, tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99, cost per 1M tokens.
[00:07:19] Avery Chen: Noted. That's exactly what we'll share.
[00:07:23] [00:07:24] Liam Patel: Next steps recap: we'll share the benchmark sheet and a config gist (Avery). You provide prompt set and traffic shape (Diego). Security will get SOC2 pack and KMS integration doc (Liam). We'll schedule a Private feasibility session (SE-led) next week.
[00:07:40] Tom Becker: Sounds good.
[00:07:42] Dr. Mira Sol: Thanks — excited to see the numbers.
[00:07:46] [00:07:50] Priya Nair: Please include a note on required contractual terms for data residency.
[00:07:55] Liam Patel: Will do.
[00:07:58] [00:08:00] Diego Ramos: One quick clarification — when you say p95 300ms, are we measuring from request received to first byte of user-visible token or to final completion?
[00:08:09] Avery Chen: Good point — usually we measure p95 to first user-token for streaming UX, and also provide full-completion p95. We'll include both.
[00:08:19] Tom Becker: Great.
[00:08:20] Liam Patel: Alright, we'll follow up with the artifacts. Thanks everyone.
[00:08:24] Meeting end: 2028-06-19T15:58:00Z
